content.question: What layout did the instructor replace ConstraintLayout with when demonstrating relative positioning?

options.text: RelativeLayout
LinearLayout
FrameLayout
GridLayout

content.explanation: He explicitly replaced the ConstraintLayout root with a RelativeLayout to demonstrate relative positioning of views.
hints: He said he is replacing constraint layout with relative layout.
RelativeLayout allows position relations between views.

content.question: Why does RelativeLayout not produce an orientation error like LinearLayout might?

options.text: Because RelativeLayout is not based on orientation; it positions views using relationships.
Because RelativeLayout automatically sets orientation='vertical' under the hood.
Because RelativeLayout is deprecated and Android ignores orientation errors for it.
Because RelativeLayout only accepts ImageView children.

content.explanation: RelativeLayout doesn't rely on an orientation attribute; instead it arranges children using positional relations (toLeftOf, below, etc.).
hints: He observed there was no orientation error with RelativeLayout.
Positioning is relation-based, not orientation-based.

content.question: The instructor divided the design into nine conceptual sections. Which of the following is NOT one of those sections?

options.text: Top Left
Center
Bottom Middle
Floating Center Right

content.explanation: He listed top left, top middle, top right, middle left, centre, middle right, bottom left, bottom middle and bottom right — 'Floating Center Right' was not part of the list.

content.question: When the instructor added two overlapping TextViews inside the RelativeLayout without constraints, what visual effect occurred?

options.text: The TextViews overlapped one another until relative position attributes were applied.
They automatically arranged horizontally with spacing.
They disappeared from the design preview.
Android Studio converted them into Buttons.

content.explanation: Without explicit relative attributes, both TextViews appeared at the same default position and overlapped; the instructor then demonstrated positioning them relative to each other.
hints: He observed they were overlapping like in ConstraintLayout when no positions were set.
Relative attributes fix overlaps by specifying relations.

content.question: Which attribute would you use to place a TextView to the left of another view in a RelativeLayout?

options.text: android:layout_toLeftOf='@id/otherView'
android:orientation='left'
android:layout_weight='left'
android:layout_marginLeft='@id/otherView'

content.explanation: The correct RelativeLayout attribute is android:layout_toLeftOf='@id/otherView' to position a view left of another.
hints: Think 'toLeftOf' style attributes.
Relative attributes reference other view ids.

content.question: Why did the two TextViews overlap when both were added with wrap_content?

options.text: Because no relative positioning attributes were provided, so both default to the same location and overlap.
Because wrap_content always forces overlap in RelativeLayout.
Because the parent layout was not visible in the preview.
Because TextViews cannot be siblings in a RelativeLayout.

content.explanation: They overlapped because no positioning relations were set; RelativeLayout requires attributes to disambiguate placement when multiple children would otherwise render at the same origin.
hints: Overlapping happens when no constraints/relations exist.
You must use attributes like toRightOf, below, centerInParent.

content.question: What did the instructor say about the imaginary grid lines used to teach positions?

options.text: They are conceptual aids only and are not present in Android Studio; don't try to add them in real layouts.
They must be drawn as Views to enable relative positioning.
They are a feature of ConstraintLayout, not RelativeLayout.
They are part of the manifest settings for layout debugging.

hints: He warned not to expect those lines in Android Studio.
They were used only for conceptual clarity.

content.question: Which attribute centers a view inside its parent in RelativeLayout?

options.text: android:layout_centerInParent='true'
android:gravity='center'
android:layout_weight='center'
android:center='true'

content.explanation: In RelativeLayout, android:layout_centerInParent='true' centers the view both horizontally and vertically inside its parent.
hints: Centering uses layout_centerInParent in RelativeLayout.
Gravity is used inside the view's content, not for RelativeLayout child placement.

content.question: When teaching relative positioning, the instructor suggested placing a TextView with id 'hello_world'. To place another TextView below it, which attribute would you use?

options.text: android:layout_below='@id/hello_world'
android:layout_toRightOf='@id/hello_world'
android:layout_alignParentLeft='@id/hello_world'
android:layout_marginTop='@id/hello_world'

content.explanation: Use android:layout_below='@id/hello_world' to place a view directly beneath another identified view in RelativeLayout.
hints: The attribute name uses 'below'.
It references the other view's id.

content.question: Which behavior differentiates RelativeLayout from ConstraintLayout according to the instructor?

options.text: RelativeLayout relies on view-to-view relations; ConstraintLayout uses explicit constraints to the parent and other anchors, often requiring more setup for flexible layouts.
RelativeLayout cannot overlap views while ConstraintLayout always overlaps them.
ConstraintLayout is identical to RelativeLayout but has a different name.
RelativeLayout requires weights for all children like LinearLayout.

content.explanation: He contrasted relative positioning (RelativeLayout) with constraint-based positioning (ConstraintLayout), noting RelativeLayout uses simpler relations while ConstraintLayout uses anchors and constraints.
hints: He compared the two and explained orientation vs relation-based layouts.
ConstraintLayout requires attaching constraints for many placements.

content.question: If two TextViews appear identical after copy-paste and might confuse observers, what trick did the instructor use to make their difference obvious?

Rename the XML file containing the TextView.
Change the font file on disk to highlight the difference.
Delete the first TextView to reveal the second.

This visually proves the copy-paste created a new element.

content.question: What should you do if two views overlap in RelativeLayout and you want one to appear to the right of the other?

options.text: Add android:layout_toRightOf='@id/otherView' on the view you want to move to the right.
Set android:orientation='horizontal' on the RelativeLayout.
Wrap both views inside a LinearLayout and hope for the best.
Increase the font size of the left view so it forces reflow.

content.explanation: Use android:layout_toRightOf='@id/otherView' to place a view to the right of another within a RelativeLayout.
hints: Use 'toRightOf' related attributes.
RelativeLayout attributes reference view ids.
